title: Homemade electrical continuity tester
summary: A simple test lamp built from a light bulb, a socket, a piece of double cable and insulating tape to find faults in any household appliance.
how_it_works: Strip both ends of the cable; wire one end to the bulb socket; leave the other two stripped probe-ends bare. With the appliance plugged in, touch the two probes to its current-entry points — if the bulb lights, the fault is inside the appliance; if it stays dark, the break is in the cable. It lets you diagnose an iron, fan, etc. without needlessly opening it.
problem: There were no commercial test instruments available to diagnose failing appliances at home.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: A near-zero-cost diagnostic instrument made from scrap, embodying the 'understand and repair before replace' principle central to circular, locally-productive cities.

title: Self-repair of a domestic electric iron
title_original: Revision y reparacion de la plancha
summary: A step-by-step procedure for opening, diagnosing and reassembling a flatiron — repairing its cord, thermostat and resistance instead of discarding it.
how_it_works: Using the homemade tester, the user isolates whether the fault is in the cable or inside the iron, then removes the back cover, thermostat knob and cube-wrench nuts to reach the parts. A broken cord is cut back, re-stripped and re-connected to the screws (or spliced and taped); the thermostat is checked for the faint click of its bimetallic strips. The book notes that only when the resistance itself is dead must one go to a workshop for the part.
problem: Replacement irons were scarce, so a single appliance had to be kept working for years.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Detailed teardown-and-repair knowledge that extends product lifespans and keeps maintenance in the household, the inverse of designed disposability.

title: Rebuilding and lubricating the ORBITA electric fan
title_original: Roturas y soluciones del ventilador ORBITA
summary: A full disassembly, lubrication and parts-repair guide for the common Cuban ORBITA/Predon fan, with exploded hand-drawn diagrams of the motor, stator, bushings and oscillation gears.
how_it_works: Because the bushings 'have a limited life but with good lubrication we can notably extend their useful life,' the guide teaches regular cleaning and greasing of bushings, oscillation box and shaft. It diagnoses specific faults — loose speed knob, seized rotor, worn oscillation pinions, a misaligned blade ('paleta desajustada') — and shows how to free the rotor by tapping the stator with a hammer while turning the shaft by hand, and to re-center or re-seat the blade. Broken internal wires from the winding to the switch are soldered or simply spliced and taped.
problem: Fans were essential in the Cuban climate and irreplaceable, so worn motors had to be revived rather than scrapped.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Shows maintenance literacy for a specific local product — exactly the open, repairable-by-design ethos a locally-productive city needs to replace throwaway consumption.

title: Homemade wood-ash lye and bar soap
title_original: Produccion artesanal de lejia y jabon en casa
summary: A method to leach lye from wood ash through a rustic funnel and combine it with animal or vegetable fats to make soap when industrial soap was unavailable.
how_it_works: A rustic funnel woven from alkali-resistant bamboo branches and lined ~3 cm thick with dry seedless grass straw acts as a filter; ash is packed in and water is added in stages (e.g. 2 litres every 1.5 hours) so lye trickles out slowly, then is filtered and decanted (~3 litres of this lye replaces 1 kg of caustic soda). The lye is then reacted with melted purified fat — tallow or coconut/corn/soy/palm oil — stirred over heat until a homogeneous mass forms, poured into cloth- or wax-paper-lined molds and cured for several weeks.
problem: Caustic soda and manufactured soap were both in short supply during the embargo and Special Period.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Closes a hygiene supply loop entirely from local waste streams (ash, cooking fat), a model bioregional substitution for an imported industrial product.

title: Homemade candles using plastic-tube molds and bottle-cap wick holders
summary: Casting candles from any available wax or tallow in improvised molds made of plastic pipe and metal bottle caps.
how_it_works: Plastic tubing (or similar) serves as the mold; flattened metal bottle caps are pierced in the center to hold and center the wick, knotted so it cannot slip and tied taut at top and bottom. Melted paraffin/wax/tallow is poured in and left about an hour before unmolding. The text notes tallow can be used but gives a poorer-quality candle.
problem: Frequent blackouts and no manufactured candles meant households needed their own light source.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Turns packaging waste (bottle caps, tubing) into reusable tooling for making light, a tidy example of repurposing the discard stream.

title: Bicycle inner-tube and tire repair with scrap material
title_original: Resuelva usted mismo algunos problemas de la bicicleta
summary: Field repairs for the bicycle — patching punctures and lining worn tires using nylon scraps, cellophane and coffee-bag bits, and substituting worn parts.
how_it_works: Punctures are found by inflating the tube in water and watching for bubbles, then patched cold or hot with ball-patch cement and a fabric scrap; over a worn casing the book advises laying '3 or 4 little pieces of nylon or cellophane' or cartridge paper from coffee bags, and a hot iron can be pressed for 4-5 minutes to melt patch material across the area. It also covers re-truing wheels by selectively tightening/loosening spokes and identifying/replacing left/right pedals by their R/L markings.
problem: With fuel gone, bicycles became primary transport, but tires, tubes and spare parts were almost impossible to buy.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Keeps the most sustainable urban vehicle running on salvaged consumables — a direct precedent for bike-centric, repair-first city mobility.

title: Improvised fishhooks from nails, thorns and wood
title_original: Anzuelos con clavos / con pedazos de espina y madera
summary: Fishing tackle fabricated from scavenged hard materials — nails bent into hooks, or barbs lashed from thorns and wood — for survival food gathering.
how_it_works: The survival chapter shows hooks bent and filed from nails, and composite hooks bound from a thorn or sharpened point lashed with cord to a wood shank, plus drag-hooks for baiting. It is paired with other low-tech fishing methods (hand-fishing in pools, spearing with a bayonet/knife lashed to a pole, muddying small ponds to drive fish up, and woven traps/corrals).
problem: In a survival or evacuation scenario there was no manufactured fishing tackle to catch protein.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Demonstrates fabricating functional tools from the lowest-grade scrap to secure food, the survival floor of distributed self-provisioning.

title: Solar oven and improvised field cookers
title_original: Estufa solar y cocinas de campana
summary: Fuel-free and low-fuel cooking devices — a solar oven that concentrates the sun's rays, and rustic earth-pit ovens — for cooking without conventional utensils or fuel.
how_it_works: The solar oven ('estufa solar,' drawn as a hinged reflective-lidded box) uses concentration of solar rays so that 'it needs no fuel at all'; the chapter also describes a rustic pit oven dug in the ground, filled with embers, the food vessel set in and covered with a layer of embers then earth so it bakes while protected from insects. It is presented alongside cooking eggs in large shells/bamboo over coals and boiling water in vessels made of lona (canvas) or tree bark kept over a low flame.
problem: In wartime or disaster conditions households would have no gas, no stoves and little or no fuel.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Solar and biomass-pit cooking are renewable, off-grid food-energy solutions that prefigure low-carbon distributed cooking infrastructure.

title: Standardized measuring with everyday containers
summary: A conversion system that turns common Cuban packaging — a mayonnaise jar, a condensed-milk can, a pencil, a thumb — into reliable units of volume, weight and length.
how_it_works: The book tabulates real equivalences, e.g. a full condensed-milk can = ~14.5 oz dry fine soil / 11.5 oz fresh water, a 'mayonesa' jar full of dry sand = 2 lb 7 oz, a pencil = 17.8 cm, a man's thumb = 3.5-3.8 cm, a shoe size in cm equals the foot length. For intermediate amounts you mark water levels on a strip of tape on a clear container and subdivide. It substitutes for absent measuring cups, scales and rulers.
problem: Households had no calibrated measuring cups, scales or rulers for cooking and making recipes.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: Repurposes the standardized waste of mass production into a shared metrology, a culturally specific hack that makes recipes and fabrication reproducible without instruments.

title: Cooking with discarded plant parts ('consomme of scraps')
title_original: Consome de desperdicios / Caminos no trillados
summary: A set of recipes that refunctionalize normally-discarded vegetable parts and foraged wild plants into food, headlined by a 1940s dietician's 'consomme of waste.'
how_it_works: The book revives a recipe a dietician literally named 'Consome de desperdicios,' boiling peels, carrot tops and skins, lettuce hearts, sweet-potato and radish leaves and potato skins into a broth. It extends this to foraged greens (bledo/amaranth, verdolaga/purslane) and to a 'sopa de vegetales especial' from purslane, amaranth and sweet-potato leaves, carrot peels and pumpkin flowers — turning what is normally thrown away into nutrition.
problem: Acute food scarcity meant nothing edible — including peels and wild weeds — could be wasted.
source: El Libro de la Familia (FabLab-ULB & Ernesto Oroza, 2019)
fabcity_relevance: A food-system precedent for valorizing the waste stream and local wild biomass, aligning with zero-waste, bioregional nutrition.
